lead: A small cube of material does not fly apart. The stresses on its six faces must balance, which forces the stress gradients to satisfy three equilibrium equations. Separately, every strain comes from how the displacement changes from point to point. These two sets are the starting point for solving a loaded body: equilibrium links stresses, and strain-displacement links strains to displacements. Together with Hooke's law they define boundary value problems in plane stress, plane strain and three dimensions. Design software uses them in finite element analysis; hand calculations use simplified forms.

blocks.text: Cut a tiny rectangular block of sides Δx, Δy, Δz from a loaded body. The face at x carries normal stress σx. The opposite face at x + Δx carries σx + (∂σx/∂x)Δx. The difference is a gradient times length. Summing forces in x and dividing by volume ΔxΔyΔz leaves the gradient terms. No body force first.

blocks.where: σx is normal stress on the x face; τxy is shear stress on the x face in the y direction; τxz is shear stress on the x face in the z direction; all stresses in N/mm² and lengths in mm.
These are the cyclic y and z forms. σy and σz are normal stresses; τyz is shear on the y face in the z direction; τxz is shear on the x face in the z direction.

blocks.text: If body force per unit volume has components X, Y, Z (N/mm³), add X to the x equation, Y to y, Z to z. Gravity on a long bar is the common case. The equations say a stress field cannot be chosen freely; it must vary in a balanced way. A uniform stress field with no body force automatically satisfies them, so the interesting cases have gradients. See 2.1 for the stress components on a face.

Let a point move by u in x, v in y, w in z, all in mm. For small strains, normal strain is the change in length per original length. A line element dx stretches by (∂u/∂x)dx, so εx = ∂u/∂x. Similarly εy = ∂v/∂y and εz = ∂w/∂z. These derivatives are dimensionless when u and x use the same unit.

blocks.where: u, v, w are displacements in x, y, z in mm; εx, εy, εz are normal strains, dimensionless.

blocks.text: Shear strain measures angle change. Two originally perpendicular lines along x and y rotate toward each other. The x line tilts by ∂v/∂x; the y line tilts by ∂u/∂y. The total decrease in angle is γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x. Both terms are needed. γxy is in radians. The cyclic forms are γyz = ∂v/∂z + ∂w/∂y and γzx = ∂w/∂x + ∂u/∂z.

blocks.where: u is displacement in x; v is displacement in y; γxy is engineering shear strain in radians.

blocks.text: The figure follows the worked example: differentiate the field, then read the strains at the point. Once εx, εy and γxy are known, principal strains follow from 2.6. Strain gauges and rosettes use this same idea in reverse, as shown in 2.7.

sections.h3: Plane stress, plane strain and the full problem

blocks.text: Plane stress keeps σz = τxz = τyz = 0 but not εz. Thin plates loaded in their plane are the usual case. Plane strain keeps εz = γxz = γyz = 0 but not σz. A long dam or tunnel section away from the ends is the usual case. Both are two-dimensional boundary value problems: equilibrium gives stress gradients, strain-displacement gives strains, and Hooke's law connects stress to strain. Boundary conditions fix the displacements or tractions on the edges.

Compatibility is the extra set of conditions that makes a strain field come from a single-valued displacement field. Only a few universities derive it; most syllabi stop at the equilibrium equations and strain-displacement relations. The full three-dimensional problem has three equilibrium equations, six strain-displacement relations and six stress-strain relations. Solving them by hand is rare; finite element software assembles and solves them numerically. Your exam usually asks you to write the equations, substitute a given displacement field, or check whether a stress field satisfies equilibrium.

examples.question: A displacement field in a thin plate is u = (3x + 1.5y) × 10⁻³ mm and v = (1.5x + 2y) × 10⁻³ mm, with x and y in mm. Find εx, εy and γxy at the point (2,1) mm.
steps: Write the displacement components: u = (3x + 1.5y) × 10⁻³ mm, v = (1.5x + 2y) × 10⁻³ mm.
Differentiate u with respect to x: ∂u/∂x = 3 × 10⁻³. Hence εx = 3 × 10⁻³ = 0.003.
Differentiate v with respect to y: ∂v/∂y = 2 × 10⁻³. Hence εy = 2 × 10⁻³ = 0.002.
Differentiate u with respect to y: ∂u/∂y = 1.5 × 10⁻³. Differentiate v with respect to x: ∂v/∂x = 1.5 × 10⁻³.
Add the two shear terms: γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x = 1.5 × 10⁻³ + 1.5 × 10⁻³ = 3 × 10⁻³ = 0.003 rad.
At (2,1) mm the derivatives are constant, so the same values apply at that point. The normal strains are dimensionless; γxy is 0.003 rad.
examples.answer: εx = 0.003, εy = 0.002, and γxy = 0.003 rad, all at (2,1) mm.
examples.check:
coef_u_x = 3e-3
coef_u_y = 1.5e-3
coef_v_x = 1.5e-3
coef_v_y = 2e-3
ex = coef_u_x
ey = coef_v_y
gxy = coef_u_y + coef_v_x
print(ex)
print(ey)
print(gxy)

traps: Forgetting the second term in γxy: γxy is ∂u/∂y plus ∂v/∂x, not either one alone.
Mixing units of displacement and length. If u is in mm and x is in m, convert before differentiating, or the strain is wrong by 1000.
Treating X, Y, Z as stresses. They are body force per unit volume, in N/mm³, while stress is N/mm².
Assuming plane stress means εz = 0. Plane stress means σz = 0; εz is generally nonzero through Poisson's ratio.
Writing equilibrium with σx itself instead of ∂σx/∂x. A uniform stress field balances without body force; gradients create the net force.

quiz.q: Write the three equilibrium equations in x, y and z with no body forces.
Define engineering shear strain γxy in terms of displacements.
quiz.a: γxy = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x, where u and v are displacements in x and y; γxy is in radians.

quiz.q: Why does γxy contain two derivative terms?
quiz.a: The x-direction line rotates by ∂v/∂x, and the y-direction line rotates by ∂u/∂y. The angle change is the sum of these two small rotations.

quiz.q: For u = (2x + y) × 10⁻³ mm and v = (x + 4y) × 10⁻³ mm, find εx, εy and γxy.
A stress field has σx = 4x + 2y N/mm², σy = 3x − y N/mm², τxy = 2xy N/mm², and other stresses zero. Check the x equilibrium equation at (1,2) with no body force.
quiz.a: ∂σx/∂x = 4; ∂τxy/∂y = 2x = 2 at x = 1. Sum = 6, not 0. Equilibrium is not satisfied; a body force X = −6 N/mm³ would be needed.

quiz.q: A student says plane stress means εz = 0. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: Plane stress means σz = 0, not εz = 0. In an isotropic material εz = −ν(σx + σy)/E, which is generally nonzero.

quiz.q: A displacement field is given. Can you find stresses from it without Hooke's law? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Strain-displacement relations give strains only. You need Hooke's law and the elastic constants to convert strains to stresses; equilibrium then checks whether those stresses balance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element packages build the strain-displacement matrix from these derivatives and write equilibrium in weak form. Compatibility leads to the Airy stress function and to displacement-based formulations. MEMS, pressure vessel and aerospace panel models start from these equations. Search next: compatibility equations, Airy stress function, plane stress versus plane strain, finite element stiffness matrix.
